name: Italian states before unification
capital: Rome, Naples, Turin, Florence and others
summary: The separate states of the Italian peninsula from the Renaissance to unification: the Papal States, the Kingdom of Naples and Sicily, Piedmont-Sardinia, Tuscany, Genoa and smaller duchies, often fought over by France, Spain and Austria.

knownFor.label: Renaissance
knownFor.note: Florence, Rome and Venice led European art.

location.value: The Italian Peninsula and its outlying islands.

terrain.value: The Alps in the north, the Po plain, the Apennine mountains down the middle and the islands of Sicily and Sardinia.

climate.value: Mediterranean in the south and along the coasts, and cooler and wetter in the north.

resources.value: Fertile farmland, silk, olive oil and wine, marble and fish.

population.value: About 10 million around 1500, rising to about 25 million by 1850 (estimates vary).

urbanisation.value: Naples, Rome, Milan, Venice, Florence and Genoa were among Europe’s largest cities.

disease.value: Plague struck repeatedly (notably in 1630 and 1656), and malaria affected marshy regions.

migration.value: Many people emigrated from the south in the late 1800s, especially to the Americas.

economicBase.value: Farming, silk, wool, banking and trade, with major cities specialising in crafts.

tradeRoutes.value: The ports of Genoa, Livorno, Venice and Naples linked Italy to the Mediterranean and beyond.

wealth.value: Rich cities and banking families contrasted with a poorer countryside, especially in the south.

moneyAndTax.value: Many currencies circulated, including the florin, scudo and ducat.

inequality.value: Great landed estates in the south and Sicily left many peasants poor.

governmentType.value: A patchwork of separate states, including kingdoms, duchies and the Papal States ruled by the pope.

keyRulers.value: Lorenzo de’ Medici. Popes. Victor Emmanuel II. Cavour.

succession.value: Many states were ruled by dynasties, while the popes were elected by cardinals.

institutions.value: The papal court (Curia), city councils, noble families and, later, foreign-run administrations.

stability.value: Italian Wars (from 1494); revolutions in the 1820s, 1830s and 1848.

eliteConflict.value: Noble families and foreign powers (France, Spain and Austria) competed for control of the peninsula.

armyAndTech.value: Mercenary armies led by condottieri were common in the 1400s, followed by foreign armies.

majorWars.value: Italian Wars (1494–1559); Italian Wars of Independence against Austria (from 1848).

territoryChange.value: Napoleon redrew the map; the Congress of Vienna (1814–15) restored the old patchwork of states.

alliancesRivals.value: Spain, France and Austria competed for control.

scienceEducation.value: Universities at Bologna and Padua, and scientists such as Galileo.

openness.value: Major trading cities connected Italy to the wider world.

communicationTransport.value: Sea trade and roads linked the states; railways began in the 1830s.

religion.value: Catholic; the pope ruled central Italy as the Papal States.

languageWriting.value: Mutually unintelligible regional dialects; Manzoni’s novel I Promessi Sposi (1840) used a standardised Tuscan.

socialStructure.value: Nobles, merchants, artisans and peasants, with the clergy as a powerful order.

sharedIdentity.value: Renaissance writers such as Dante and Machiavelli hoped for a united Italy, but most people spoke local dialects and lacked national feeling.

dailyLife.value: Most people were farmers, eating bread, pasta, vegetables and wine.

neighbours.value: France, Swiss, Austria, Venice, Ottoman Empire across the sea.

ideasReligions.value: Italian nationalism (the Risorgimento), spread by Mazzini and secret groups such as the Carbonari.

colonisation.value: Spanish Habsburgs ruled southern Italy and Milan until the War of the Spanish Succession (1701–14); Austria later dominated, directly ruling Lombardy–Venetia after 1815.

riseSignals.value: The Italic League treaty (1454) and Medici foreign policy were early signs of unity.

peakPeriod.value: The High Renaissance (about 1490–1530), when Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael worked.

declineSignals.value: After the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis (1559), parts of Italy fell under Spanish Habsburg control.

outcome.value: United as the Kingdom of Italy in 1861; Rome became the capital in 1871.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
